speechtext:
I do not accept that at all. That is not a question of privilege. The Minister of Finance has a responsibility to the Canadian people to be in this House to listen to the arguments of hon. members. I have attempted to consider the white paper-or what the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) referred to as the "red manifesto"-on the basis of its effects upon Canadian taxpayers, its equity, its fairness of tax distribution, as well as something that the Ontario Economic Council refers to as incentives in the tax structure. These incentives relate to the proposed reforms that govern the extent to which our economy can expand, as well as the extent to which individuals exercise their
Taxation Reform
ingenuity and eagerness and display aggressiveness in developing their own businesses. In other words, when I think of incentives I think of fattening the animal, of building a little more muscle in the Canadian economy, so we can afford to pay for those services that the Canadian people deserve and demand.
If the Minister of Finances reads my speech, I hope he will not think I am being partisan when I say that I can find no way in which the white paper succeeds to any measurable extent on either count, whether in terms of equity or in terms of incentive. With regard to fairness of the tax distribution, in other words equity, having listened to the Minister of National Revenue and to the speeches of a number of other ministers, including the Minister of Finance, I am still convinced that the small increase in the basic exemption does nothing more than cloud the issue, befuddling the Canadian taxpayer into thinking he is getting a break. In actual fact it is nothing more than an increase in taxation; and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has done a masterful job in pointing out the effects the tax changes will have upon the average Canadian. By the end of two years when these tax proposals come into effect, inflation will have eaten away most of the benefits. Why are these benefits not brought in now? Why do we have to wait for two years if we are interested in helping the little man?
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
What about the tax credits to which the Leader of the Opposition referred? This appears to have quite a bit of relevance. Why was the alternative of '"tax credits" not considered and recommended to the committee for study? Let me leave that point, Mr. Speaker, because there are a number of other members who want to talk about that.
I am interested in the consideration of the effects of the white paper on the Atlantic provinces. This is a poor area in Canada about which we have had numerous discussions. In this regard, we must consider the unemployment situation. In consideration of the measures proposed in the white paper I think that if many of the proposals are implemented the Atlantic provinces might just as well forget about Confederation. That area of Canada will be at such a disadvantage it will literally have to close shop. The minister reminds me of a hibernating bear when he talks about these tax proposals. He thinks the Canadian nation will literally live off its own

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
fat. There are no incentives and the proposals in the white paper must be considered as being disadvantageous to Atlantic Canada.
What kind of an economy do we have at the present moment in Atlantic Canada? We have the highest unemployment rate of any part of this country and reference has been made to this fact. Let me mention two or three statistics to verify this fact. These statistics do not exaggerate the situation, as a matter of fact, the situation is worse than the statistics suggest.
In October 1967 we had 4 per cent unemployment in Atlantic Canada. The situation was actually worse than the statistics indicate. I understand the sampling procedure used by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics does not accurately reflect unemployment. In October 1967 we had 4 per cent unemployment and in 1969 we have 5.2 per cent unemployment. In October 1967 New Brunswick had slightly more than 3 per cent unemployed, yet in October of 1969 it had 5.7 per cent. In October of 1967, Newfoundland had over 5 per cent unemployment and in 1969 has 7.4 per cent, the highest level since I was born a Canadian.
Again, we have a tight money situation in the Atlantic provinces. When there is a tight money situation in Canada we see the effect immediately. Investors do not want to move into areas where there is speculation and risk. Again, the economy of our area is related directly to small businesses which suffer a very high mortality rate. This area is made up mostly of small businesses. We do not have many of the large corporate clusters like metropolitan areas of Toronto. Montreal and Pittsburgh have. We have a multiplicity of small businesses. This is the economic fibre of that part of Canada.
Let us consider the type of economy we enjoy and the effect the proposals contained in this white paper will have on Atlantic Canada. Small construction firms build apartment blocks, houses and so on. Under the present tax system there is an incentive in respect of capital cost allowances. Now when they are faced with this recapturing clause that will apply to each property independently they will no longer have incentive to expand their operations. I hope there will be changes made when the committee studies this white paper. The minister suggests that the loophole under present recapturing arrangements will be plugged. This will remove that incentive and force each proper -

ty owned by a business man, to stand on its own merit. When these small construction companies sell a property they will face the recapturing clause immediately. This proposed change will make it impossible for the small construction firms to expand or get into new business. They will pretty well have to retain existing properties. This is the "disincentive" about which I am talking.
Again, in the past some small builders have, as a result of ingenuity and effort, been able to build houses for resale at a profit of $10,000 or $12,000 in respect of a real expensive home, or $4,000 to $5,000 on a lower priced home. This present proposal will completely eliminate the incentive for these people to get involved.
I could not go on without reference to the Home Owner's tax, a tax which will be applied to a man if the sells his home and makes a profit. I really cannot see the advantage to Canadians of this aspect of the white paper. On the contrary, I think this will put many people in a mess. This is true because of the administrative costs and red tape involved. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not want to go into the bedrooms of the nation, but he is coming damn close to doing so as a result of this proposal. The Government is forcing Canadians to be materialistic. They are becoming the victims of government involvement in their own affairs. The government is trying to play the role of a political pinnochio when it sticks its nose into the affairs of every Canadian. As a result of government red tape the average Canadian is no longer a free man in his own home. A man's home used to be his castle. It is now becoming merely a piece of property. I could go on and on in this regard, but time does not permit me to do so.
Reference was made earlier to small business. The Atlantic provinces are made up of small businesses. With the elimination of the 21 per cent concessional provision, the small businesses will now have to compete with large corporate businesses. I have in mind small lumber dealers as well as primary, secondary and tertiary industries which net $20,000 or $30,000 per year employing 25 to 30 people more or less. These companies are already faced with stiff competition. They are also faced with the difficulty of raising funds. Banks have tightened up and are demanding high collateral. These firms can no longer get the money they need to expand and develop markets. They face difficulties not faced by big companies. As well there is a great deal
December 1. 1969

Taxation Reform
of speculation involved in small business ventures and a very high mortality rate.
In view of the present proposals of the minister, these small businesses will have to close shop. They will be faced with a 50 per cent tax if they make $20,000 to $30,000 a year or more. I am amazed that there is not a greater conflict between the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). One minister, the minister of Regional Economic Expansion, recognizes that incentives must be provided to small businessmen in the four Atlantic provinces who want to expand. In the case of a company which plans to expand and invest $30,000 there is a 20 per cent incentive. If such a company wishes to establish a new business costing $60,000 or more it receives a 20 per cent incentive. These companies must face initial high labour costs and the new Regional Development Department is to help with these costs.
In spite of this recognition by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, the Minister of Finance takes an opposite view. One minister says we should not discourage small businesses from getting on their feet, yet the other uses the excuse that small businessmen ought not to be encouraged by the 21 per cent concessional arrangement. We have become involved in a political push-me-pull-you. The Government is moving in both directions. One minister wants to build incentives into the Atlantic economy while the other minister is cutting his legs out from under him. I should like to tune in on cabinet discussions when this matter is considered.
A great deal of the employment in the Atlantic provinces is created by the exploration of extractive industries, namely the mining operations. This is where a lot of our growth has taken place in the last few years. Recently I read in the Ontario Economic Council report that there has been one billion dollars annually put into the Canadian economy by oil and mining companies through exploration work. A great percentage of that has been investment in northern parts of Canada. Much has been invested in Quebec, Labrador, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick where there is a great deal of undeveloped resources. In other words, the aim should be to build incentives in these areas to encourage industry to Atlantic Canada to develop our resources.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In other words, there should be extra incentives for companies which are willing to gamble and explore. If they make good, they are really protected. But this white paper, if it should be accepted, would eliminate practically any incentive to a mining operation to move into an area in which there is a danger of failure. It eliminates the three-year protective tax agreements which have been in existence. This will really disrupt mining in Atlantic Canada. The government says, "If you move in and do not make it, thanks anyway; if you do make it, pay up". The government says, "If you pay for your capital and operating costs, then start paying your taxes". In other words, there is no real incentive to large companies to move into areas in which there is a need for development and where there should be incentives.
I could refer at length to evidence in support of my position if time permitted. However, I shall refer to something which perhaps is of great concern to some people. In reply to the hon. member who mentioned that the provinces are very dissatisfied the minister said, "Refer to Table 13." I have referred to it. It indicates that every province will get an increase as a result of this proposal and that there will be $165 million generated by the tax proposals. You may refer to page 85 for that statistic. The government says that, as a government, it is prepared to give all 10 provinces a total of $20.4 million. I am not a mathematician, but it seems to me that is $20 million to the provinces and $145 million to the federal government, which means the federal government receives 88 cents out of every dollar and that the provinces combined receive 12 cents.
I have computed the average percentage of increase to the provinces. These are the percentages of increase in income tax going to the provinces along with the equalization payments: Newfoundland less than .5 per cent. The province of Nova Scotia will receive an increase of .8 per cent from Ottawa on the basis of the income tax and equalization payments. Prince Edward Island will receive .8 per cent; New Brunswick .7 per cent; Quebec, .6 per cent; Ontario, .6 per cent; Manitoba, 1.2 per cent; Saskatchewan, .6 per cent; Alberta, 1.5 per cent and British Columbia, 1 per cent. This represents an average increase of less than 1 per cent. The provinces are supposed to be satisfied with this amount. There is no reference to the need for reviewing the tax-

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
sharing arrangements with the provinces. How can one blame the premiers of the various provinces for expressing regret at the almost complete contempt the federal government has shown for the provinces. This is really discouraging. At the Hot Springs conference when the Prime Minister was asked about the provinces, the Prime Minister said he would tell the provinces that perhaps they ought to consider doubling their taxes. This is the federal formula for helping the provinces-one times two, double your taxes. This is what the Prime Minister tells the provinces. He tells them that if they want services they should double their taxes. How can they double their taxes in the face of these income tax increases, as well as other increases by the federal government.
If this white paper is to make sense, it would seem to me there should be some study of the tax-sharing arrangement with the provinces. This is not a reform of our tax structure. As a new member I expected some proposals to change the balance of our tax structure in Canada. This is a disguise for an increase in taxation.
I could continue and give more details, but I wish to sum up my feelings about the impact of the white paper on Atlantic Canada. First, it will force the provinces to increase their taxes because of the heavy demands for new services and the imposition of certain programs by the federal government which the federal government plans to vacate, in some cases by the year 1975 and earlier in other cases. It will pretty well ruin the small businessman in Atlantic Canada. It will discourage mining exploration and in that sense will lessen the opportunities of Atlantic Canada to develop its resources. It will bring about a substantial increase in the number of unemployed which is now being increased by present government policies.
I see that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) is blushing. I can appreciate the reason he is blushing. It is because of the lack of support he receives from his cabinet in his efforts to improve the situation in Atlantic Canada. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion could not take it; he stayed away. There will be an increase in unemployment in Atlantic Canada, a situation which is chronic because of present government policy. There will be a reduction in the standard of living and a dampening of incentive. There will be a need for more welfare because fewer people will be employed. All I can say is that from now on I hope for goodness sake the government will very seri-

ously consider the need for an increase in regional disparity grants. There will have to be an increased effort to feed the people of Atlantic Canada because this is what the government will have to do if some of the basic tenets of this proposed white paper are adopted.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the Motion of Mr. Benson (for Mr. Macdonald, Rosedale):
December 1, 1969
That the white paper entitled Proposals for Tax Reform tabled in the House on November 7, 1969, be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to follow my good friend from Gander-Twillingate, but I was considerably disturbed to hear the hon. member who is from Newfoundland criticize to such a great extent the white paper on tax reform because it has been my thought that the white paper was designed to help the low income provinces.
It was with a great deal of interest that I listened to the speech given in this House on Friday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). The minister, as usual, was well prepared and articulate as he outlined the proposals for tax reform. Let me say now that I believe the great majority of those proposals are sound and will shortly be the basis for excellent legislation which will recast our present outdated tax structure in a form more in line with the concept of fairness and justice which most Canadians desire.
Lest the minister get too comfortable, I should warn the House that this is the last kind word I will speak about the white paper today. My concern is with the plight of the small businessman. When we talk about the small businessman in Canada we are talking about a man who, to complement his ingenuity and resourcefulness, often works 10 or 12 hours a day. We are talking about a man who finds himself competing with large firms, many of which are international or even multi-national in character. He is a man who cuts short his summer vacation, if he has any at all, in order to return home to deal with his business problem; a man who rises from the supper table and heads, not for the t.v. set but for the den to work out business problems; a man who must fight long and hard to keep his small part of the market. The small businessman in Canada stands as a living example of the difference between socialism and free enterprise. Let us not take from this man, who has pride in both the growth of his company and his country, the incentives which he needs to carry on his business. At present, the tax rate is 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of corporate earnings and 50 per cent on any amount over that. If the proposals in the white paper were to be adopted, the 21 per cent tax rate would ultimately be abolished and the 50 per cent rate would apply on
Taxation Reform
total corporate income. This would be disastrous for Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) proposed that the new 50 per cent rate be phased in over five years with the 21 per cent rate applying only to the initial $28,000 in the first year, $21,000 in the second, $14,000 in the third, $7,000 in the fourth, and be eliminated in the fifth year.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Why has this new so-called reform been suggested? In his speech to the House on Friday, the minister gave his answer to this question. He believes that the main reason Canadians set up corporations is to avoid tax. My belief is that this is not the case. I believe that there are many reasons for setting up corporations, but the most acceptable is to limit the liability of the persons involved.
The small businessman does not seek to avoid paying taxes. He merely wants to remain in such a position as to be able to use his profits to expand and improve his operation, in other words, to re-invest in the country. Are we to stop this re-investment? After all, the small businessman does not realize any immediate personal gain or see any instant improvement in his own standard of living by plowing profits back into the company. He needs this capital to enable his small corporation-a Canadian corporation- to develop and enlarge, perhaps by purchasing more sophisticated equipment to produce a superior product.
However, I realize that there may be some persons who, under the present tax structure, have made a practice of leaving corporate income for an indefinite period of time in the company, particularly in a closely held corporation or series of such corporations which boast incomes of $35,000 or less. Clearly, in such cases the tax revenue of the country suffers because the corporate profits are only being taxed at the rate of 21 per cent.
What is the solution? I propose that the solution is not to tax 50 per cent, which cuts down the incentive. I propose that the closely held corporations which have incomes of $35,000 or less be allowed to retain the present 21 per cent tax rate for five year periods. At the end of any given five year period, the businessman would be taxed on the profit of each consecutive year in the period at the rate he would have been taxed had his corporate income been treated as personal income. In other words, the small businessman would only be deferring his payment of taxes. He

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
could not avoid payment. For the privilege of delaying tax payment he would pay interest to the government on the amount of the deferred taxes at the rate of 1 per cent above the long-term borrowing rate of the federal government. It would also be stipulated that to benefit under this deferred taxation plan a corporation would have to be at least 51 per cent Canadian owned.
I feel that my proposal is a good compromise between the recommendations in the white paper, which would lead to greatly restricted growth of existing Canadian small corporations as well as to the discouragement of individuals with exciting ideas from going into business for themselves, and the present legislation which admittedly is open to some abuse. The solution I put forward in my brief remarks today would allow legitimate businessmen with closely held corporations to retain the internal source of expansion capital they so desperately need to compete, while at the same time not reducing over-all the taxation revenue due our country.
In conclusion, I would like to read from an editorial entitled ''Profit and Loss" which appeared in the November 11 issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail. It reads as follows:
Canadians cannot know how much of their productivity and prosperity has depended upon creative men who started small, with the aid of the low 21 per cent rate, and eventually grew big and forced their competitors to grow also, and thereby provided wealth and jobs all round.
All the Canadian small businessman wants is to be allowed a chance to survive and the opportunity to grow. My hope is that the minister will not decide to take away that chance of growth.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much has been said about the good features of the white paper on tax reform-mostly by the minister-that the public is in no danger of overlooking them. Indeed, after his prodigious efforts in promoting this particular package of payments, the minister could well take on the job of advertising the advantages of bikinis to the belles of Baffin land. Probably it would prove an even more agreeable task than winging his way across Canada accompanied by the white paper.
In any event, I shall say at the outset that there are measures in the white paper which distribute the tax burden a little more fairly, and where these exist we favour them as far as they go. But the net result falls far short

of an equitable and effective taxation policy for Canada. I am glad of this opportunity to indicate some of the reasons.
In his speech opening the debate the other day, the Minister of Finance said that people in the middle income group of taxpayers want to be sure that those in the upper income group are pulling their fair share of the load. If middle income taxpayers need this assurance, it is doubly necessary for those in the low income groups, and extremely urgent for those who do not get enough income to be taxed at all. For it is only when those in the upper brackets are paying their full share of taxes that those on low incomes can keep their heads above water. Fair taxation of the wealthy is the only way to provide the public goods and services which alone can prevent the cancer of poverty from spreading in this country.
In the opinion of the New Democratic Party, the proposals of the white paper do not ensure taxation according to ability to pay, nor will the imposition of a capital gains tax redress the balance. As long as there is a ceiling on the tax rate, we shall not have taxation according to ability to pay. We do not intend to settle for anything less than the removal of the ceiling.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Various ideas have been given in this debate about criteria to be kept in mind when designing a tax system. Our deputy leader gave an admirable summary of our ideas the other day. But I would like to add just one more thought. To me, the most important thing is not how much you pay in taxes; it is how much you have left to live on after you have paid your taxes. Judged by this standard, taxpayers in the upper brackets will not have too much to worry about, not if the recent statements of bank incomes and corporation profits mean anything. Judged by this standard, however, there are a lot of people in the low income brackets who do have plenty to worry about, to say nothing of those millions of Canadians below the taxation and poverty levels altogether.
The Economic Council says that one Canadian in five is living below the poverty level now. That verb "living" is inaccurate. The proper one is existing, and existing in a state of insecurity and misery impossible for any of us in this chamber to comprehend. In today's conditions, the minister's suggestion of $30 a week provides the kind of existence
December 1, 1969

that no modern prison or penitentiary would dare to tolerate. In this connection it is interesting to note a reference in today's Globe and Mail to the minister's visit to Vancouver. It shows that his hotel suite there cost $45 daily, in other words enough to keep a $30 a week man for a week and a half, yet that was merely for lodging in the hotel room for one night.
The minister boasted that the white paper will take three quarters of a million taxpayers off the rolls because of their poverty. The Economic Council says poverty begins for a single person below $1,800, and for a family of four below $4,200. Senior citizens' organizations and others have been campaigning long and hard for income tax exemptions of $2,000 for single persons and $4,000 for married couples. Yet the minister sets the new exemptions at only $1,500 a year for a single person and $3,500 for a family of four. What kind of justice is this? What kind of sense? It has been said that you cannot get blood from a stone. Well, the minister is having a good try. What he fails to recognize is that these poverty striken taxpayers are not stones. They are men and women of flesh and blood and feelings, and have the same kind of needs as the rest of us.
The proposed exemptions should be raised, and raised well above poverty level. Our recent New Democratic Party Convention in Winnipeg put our policy in a resolution in these words:
Tax reform to make the over-all tax system truly progressive: integration of the income tax system with the minimum income so that no income taxes are paid by persons below the poverty level and the income tax form can be used for determining eligibility for the minimum income.
The minimum income? That brings me to another point of criticism of the white paper, a point which has been dealt with already but which needs much emphasis. You cannot make a proper assessment of the value of these proposals without knowing what other proposals the government is going to make in interrelated fields.
What is the government going to do about the rising cost of living? Establishing boards, councils,, committees, task forces and other similar pieces of machinery is not action. It is merely buying time for inaction. The public, and the members of Parliament here who are their representatives, need to know what is going to be done to stop inflation and rising living costs. They need to know in order to pass judgment on the validity of the white
Taxation Reformpaper proposals. Yet all our inquiries in this direction are met by smiling secretiveness. The masterpiece will be unveiled in due course. Meanwhile it is government property. Keep out! The taxpayers are beginning to get tired of this. They have paid for the machinery. They want to know what, if anything, is going on. They have a right to get value for their money.
A second question relevant to the proposals in the white paper is: what is the government going to propose at the end of its long review of existing social security programs? Is it going to penny pinch still further by applying the means test to all of them? Is it going to face reality by making long-overdue increases? Is it going to replace the outmoded patchwork by a guaranteed income?
The Prime Minister's recent answer to that question when I asked it was not too reassuring. He said, "... as a government we are not yet satisfied that this is a realistic step." Not realistic? With four and a half million Canadians existing below the poverty line, with all that such an appalling figure indicates in the way of public taxation for unnecessary social assistance, disease, delinquency, crime, divorce, drugs, mental breakdown, and ultimately the outbreak of civil disorder in our great cities.
Not realistic? With the average gross income of a manufacturing worker only $5,723, and his family exposed to the hazards of unemployment and all the other risks which become so acute where income leaves no margin. Not realistic? How realistic is this government? And how long will it refuse to face reality in the matter of a fair distribution of income?
If this is the government's answer, what other social security proposals does it have in mind? If we are to assess the proposals in the white paper we need to know. Then, there is the sales tax. What does the government intend to do about it? For years now the public has been clamouring to get rid of it as a brake on production, with particular reference to housing. We need to know the answer to this one, too.
Undoubtedly these and many other relevant questions will be raised when the white paper is in committee. Until the answers are provided the public can get no accurate and comprehensive idea of the effect of the white paper proposals on the individual taxpayer and on the state of our economy as a whole. What is the sense in granting increased

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
exemptions if the cost of living and other kinds of taxes are going to gobble up the increases?
One feature that we in this party deplore is that the white paper proposals perpetuate the double standard of income tax deductions which exists in our present tax laws. There is one standard for the self-employed, the professional and business taxpayer, who can deduct all sorts of costs as expenses of earning his income. There is quite another for the wage and salary earner who can deduct practically nothing. True, the white paper proposes a slight easement for the wage and salary earner, 3 per cent of his income, with a maximum amount deductible of $150 a year. But for the self-employed there is still no maximum to the amount he can deduct.
Nowhere does this double standard of deductibility show up more glaringly than in the new proposal of child care expenses for working parents. Let me say at once that we welcome the idea of helping working parents bear the burden of expense for their children while they, the parents, are working. The proposal to pay up to $500 per year per child under the age of 14 is one small and very belated step to protect family life. But upon examination it is really a very limited one.
Why cannot a working mother, a taxpayer, deduct the actual cost of child care as an expense of earning her income in the same way as the self-employed taxpayer can do with his expenses? Surely, if the principle is right in the one case it is right in the other. The new child-care provision is thus manifestly discriminatory against the working mother who earns a wage or salary. Alimony and child care payments made by men have always been tax deductible. Why not babysitting or nursery school expenses for women?
The white paper proposal sets a limit of $2,000 per family for child care services. In other words, the government is saying clearly to parents across Canada, "Four children is enough." I am inclined to agree. But what about existing families of five or six or more children, children in mother-led or single parent families where the need for child care is great?
You will say, of course, that if a woman or a parent has a number of small children her place is at home, bringing them up. Bringing them up on what? Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we have here a powerful argument for the measure I have urged in this house on

a number of occasions-the provision of an allowance which would permit mothers of young children to stay at home and look after them instead of having to take jobs outside the home to get enough to feed and clothe them and keep them in decent surroundings. Such a measure has been in effect in France for a number of years now. I would hope that our government would soon consider this kind of family protection for Canada. If it will not do it for the family, let it do it for the taxpayers who have to pay all the costs of neglected homes and neglected children.
Another shortcoming of the white paper child-care proposal is that the $500 figure bears no relation to the actual cost of child care. One organization of single parents, Single Parents Associated, with headquarters in Toronto, summarizes the actual cost per year of child care service for one child. The figures are based on a 50-week year and enumerate the various forms of child-care which now exist: live-in help $4,200 per child; daily help $3,550 per child; outside day care $1,000 per child; nursery school $1,680 per child; and private school $3,000 per child. Obviously the white paper has not priced the actual cost of child care before setting its tax deduction figure because the two have no relation to each other. Further, it is true that every single form of child-care service enumerated is in short supply and would have to be greatly augmented if even a small fraction of the children of working parents were to be adequately protected.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
One further criticism of this child-care proposal that is the need to keep receipts in order to qualify for the deduction. It seems to me that this is an almost insurmountable and quite unnecessary obstacle. Working parents and the baby sitters they employ are just not geared for such paper work which is the delight of public servants like those in the minister's department. The income tax form clearly sets out the occupation of the taxpayer and the number of his or her dependants. Why not permit him or her simply to deduct a definite amount per year for child care, in the same way that for years all taxpayers were permitted to deduct a flat $100 for medical expenses? To me, this would seem a much simpler way to do it.
There are many more things Mr. Speaker, I should like to say about the white paper if time permitted. But I want to end with just one more observation which seems to me very
December 1, 1969

important. A greal deal is said about the serious consequences of endangering incentive by taxing the upper income brackets their full share. We are told it would be fatal to the future of Canada to make these taxpayers feel that their efforts were going to be curbed. I have come to believe that there is a far greater danger in frustrating the initiative of the people at the lower end of the income scale. A great many of these people have never had a chance to exercise that initiative and in too many cases it is atrophied. The cost to the taxpayer of carrying these people along in idleness because their initiative cannot find an outlet, is very great. Too many children are growing up who have never known what initiative is because their parents, too, were born and raised in poverty and insecurity. They have no chance to exercise their initiative and no incentive to do the sort of thing that is natural to people in higher income groups. How can such children be expected to develop initiative? The very limited success of the Head Start Program and other programs designed to coax out this almost dead initiative in children has indicated the seriousness of allowing this to be stifled at the source.
To my mind we need an income tax policy which, by taxing according to ability to pay, right up to the top of the income scale, will encourage the initiative of those low income citizens whose efforts could add so much to their own lives and the life of this country. I do not believe this white paper provides such a policy.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate on tax reform proposals though, in my opinion, it seems somewhat premature and this for two main reasons. The first one is that it was absolutely impossible in the short time we have had at our disposal since the white paper was tabled to assimilate it entirely and to understand fully all the recommendations it contains. The second reason is that it might perhaps have been more appropriate for us to hear from the various agencies that might have wished to submit briefs.
The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Canadian Bar Association, the Chambre de Commerce, the Board of Trade intend to submit briefs which, I am sure of it, would have been very useful to the members of the House before they got ready to take part in the debate.
Taxation Reform
As far as I am concerned, I am interested in talking about these problems, both as a member of parliament and as an accountant. My constituents in the riding of Laurier are poor people, but they nevertheless were pleased with some recommendations, particularly the one relating to basic personal exemptions that are increased from $1,000 to $1,400 for single people and from $2,000 to $2,800 for married people as well as the exemption that applies to working parents. In such a case, a deduction would be allowed for child care expenses, up to $500 per child under 14 years of age, or 2,000 per family.
They are also satisfied with the one allowing a deduction of 3 per cent of the salary for professional expenses up to a maximum of $150.
Mr. Speaker, some years ago I had an opportunity to take part in a debate and I chose to speak on the report prepared by the Belanger Commission after its study of possible tax reforms in the province of Quebec. I then opposed the capital gains tax and I used as main argument that it might keep eventual investors away.
However, considering the new philosophy established by the minister in the proposals for tax reform, I have to side with him, because, at the present time, the point is priority and equity for the Canadian taxpayers. At the beginning of the paper entitled "Main points", it is said and I quote:
A number of goals and standards have guided the government in its approach to reform. They include a fair distribution of the tax burden based upon ability to pay; ... steady economic growth and continuing prosperity; the understanding of modern social needs... a system that can and will be used by the provinces.
Naturally, the minister immediately states that the co-operation of the provinces will be needed if we are to be in a position to apply the recommendations that will be made. It would therefore be fitting that we meet with the provinces for a joint conference on the recommendations of the white paper and that we endeavour to find a uniform tax system for the country, that would be equally applicable to the provinces.
As an accountant, I naturally have a number of questions that I would like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in order to obtain more information about certain matters which, at the present time, appear rather obscure.

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Recommendation 5.5 of the white paper
says:
The government proposes to create a new depreciation class which would sweep up all of these nothings and would enable the taxpayer to deduct 10 per cent of the book value of this class each year.
The first question would be: What does the minister mean by the book value? It would seem advisable to me that the minister give us, whenever he feels it is the right moment, a definition of the expression "book value", so that we can understand the exact meaning of the recommendations when they are approved, with or without amendment.
It is proposed that 10 per cent of the book value of assets be deducted each year, but it is not said whether this deduction will apply on a direct line basis or whether it will be calculated on the basis of the residual value, as is the case now throughout the nation. This is another element to consider and on which to obtain more explanations.
What surprises me somewhat is that recommendation 5.14 again mentions depreciation, and I quote:
Therefore, the government intends in due course to invite briefs on the system and rates of capital cost allowance.
Yet, if we are revising all the rates, it may have been somewhat premature to set a 10 per cent rate, as we would like to know the views of experts in this field before setting or revising rates.
Recommendation 5.8 concerns the selling of goodwill, and I quote:
-taxpayers who sell goodwill in the first year of the new system would be taxable on 40 per cent ... if in the second year, taxable on 45 per cent and exempt on 55 per cent; and so on, with the taxable portion increasing by 5 percentage point each year until the thirteenth year-
Now, it would seem, at first sight, that such a way of taxing the selling of goodwill is not very equitable, that the 40 per cent tax is arbitrary and that, consequently, it might be appropriate to know the reasons behind it.
If an individual sells his shares instead of the goodwill, it would seem that the tax would not apply and, consequently, there could be an injustice with regard to the sale of the goodwill. I wonder why we could not, when the minister sets evaluation day, evaluate the goodwill of the various business concerns according, naturally, to recognized accounting criteria.
[Mr. Leblanc (Laurier).l
What about the criterion whereby the number of years during which the business has existed should be taken into account? Indeed, if an individual has been in business for five years, he could perhaps spread the tax over a five-year period; he could do the same if he has been in business for ten years, perhaps at a maximum rate of 5 per cent per year. On the other hand, the tax levied could go from zero to 5 per cent per year; thus after a 20-year period the whole amount would become taxable.
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some confusion, or at least the translation of some articles would seem to be misleading. I should like to mention, in particular, recommendation 3.20 which says in French:
... le Gouvernement propose que les contribua-bles qui, en raison de leurs occupations profes-sionnelles, sont appeles 4 se deplacer d'une region a une autre au Canada, soient autorises a consi-derer la vente de leur maison et l'achat d'une autre residence dans la nouvelle region comme une transaction non imposable, ...
The English text is somewhat different. It might be advisable to know which text is the right one. This is what we have in English, and I quote:

In addition to the exemption, the government proposes that a taxpayer who moves from one area to another within Canada in connection with a change of job-

In French, the term "change of job" has been translated as follows:
-en raison de leurs occupations professionnel-les,-
Does it actually mean therefore that the individual should also change jobs or whether he only has to move from one city to another. For instance, if the comptroller of a large company in Montreal was called back to the head office in Ontario, in order to perform the same duties would it be considered as a change of job or a transfer for professional purposes?
This could apply to salesmen as well as to accountants or lawyers who, for one reason or another, must travel from one province to another in order to do their job.
As to recommendations 5.46 and 5.47, the English text is much more precise than the French text.
Recommendation 5.47 reads as follows, and I quote:
December 1, 1969

En consequence, le Gouvernement propose que ces contribuables soient autorises a echelonner la declaration de ces sommes sur plusieurs annees. En d'autres termes, ils les feraient figurer dans leurs revenus declares a mesure que diminueraient leurs creances et leurs stocks.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Now the English text says-and I quote:

Specifically, they would bring them into income as their total outstanding receivables and inventories are reduced.

So the English text contains the word "total" which does not appear in the French text. As to the word "outstanding", it means exactly what the government has in mind but it does not seem to be translated faithfully in French.
By the way, the C.C.H. produced recently hypothetical model figures about the recommendation to place the book-keeping system of business men and professional people on an annually increasing basis instead of maintaining the present collection basis.
The C.C.H. gives the following example: If there are $25,000 in bills receivable in 1970, they will have to be entered in the books and in 1971 there would be bills totalling $40,000. There would be at the end of the year $30,000 in bills receivable and $35,000 in cash received.
One would have to know the exact taxable amount, as there seems to be some confusion among accountants as to this. Indeed, the figures published by the C.C.H. are merely an interpretation and are not necessarily the same as the ones obtained by some accountants.
I believe it is important that this matter be cleared up. If professional people and non incorporated owners have to set up their accounting system on a new basis, will they benefit from the same exemptions that are granted to corporations, especially as concerns pension fund contributions for current and past services, since corporations may deduct from their income tax their payments in that regard under contracts signed with their employees. Professional people cannot, at the present time, deduct them.
If we require equitably professional people and other businessmen who are not incorporated to pay taxes according to another system, we could perhaps grant them the
Taxation Reform
same exemptions that can exist, particularly in relation to the pension funds, for current and past services.
Chapter 4 deals with the granting of a fiscal benefit to shareholders. Indeed, a shareholder who receives a dividend will also obtain from the corporation a credit that will be proportionate to the taxes that have been paid.
This is obviously an advantage as far as promotion is concerned. It amounts, I think, to an incentive to industry as a whole. There is perhaps the danger of some difficulties arising in the bond market because those who will get interest will have absolutely no credit that might minimize the amount which they receive in that way as interest. And we can wonder if these people will buy the bonds issued by the three levels of government and by the school boards since they will have no credit to offset their amount of taxes. This could perhaps bring about-if my assumption is correct-an increase in the rate of interest in order to find buyers. Thus, if you increase the rate of interest for the municipalities, you might get an increase in taxes, in rents and finally in the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, due to all my other tasks, it was impossible for me to go through this white paper. I agree with its main philosophy, which is to ensure the imposition of a fair share of taxation based on the ability to pay, and I hope that we shall soon be more enlightened on this matter, after the Minister of Finance will have given us additional particulars and after hearing the various briefs that the experts intend to submit to the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in any discussion of a matter as important as tax reform I am sure consideration as to the reasons for such reform and the events leading up to it is vital to an understanding of the situation presently brought to the attention of the House by the government. I shall confine my remarks pretty well to general observations, consistent with the limited time at my disposal, and I should like to consider first of all the first chapter of the white paper, the document which has been referred to as a red manifesto.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext: By whom?

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
I did not say by whom. I said it had been referred to as such, and that

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
was a proper statement of fact. Under the heading Tax Reform, the imposition of a fair share of taxation based on the ability to pay is mentioned as the objective of the tax proposals. I rather object to soaking the person who has the ability to pay. It seems to me there should be considerations other than just the ability to pay; there is more to it than that.
Ability to pay is derived from the willingness of individuals to work to earn money and to acquire that ability. It does not just happen, and I do not think it should be taken for granted by any government. I feel that the person who has made an extraordinary effort should not necessarily be discriminated against. I am thinking, now, of the individual who has ambition for himself and for his family and who possesses a desire to improve, create and accomplish something.
Surely such a person deserves special encouragement rather than simply being soaked, which is the suggestion in this paragraph of the white paper. Why should he be penalized? This is a point which the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray), representing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) here this afternoon, might well bear in mind when the subject is further examined. I urge the government not to be induced into applying the principle embodied in the ability to pay theory. It is not automatic; government must be careful not to kill the goose which lays the golden egg; it should not discourage ambitious people. There are some who are willing to make the utmost use of the opportunities which present themselves, and there are others who do not possess such ambition. To my mind, the function of a government is to create a climate of opportunity and then encourage the individual to take advantage of it.
The phrase "tax reform" pretty well suggests a necessity for taxation. Under our system, taxation is essential inasmuch as it provides for the needs of government. Whether this is a good thing or not does not come into the question at the moment; it is simply a fact under our system. The state today is taking more and more of the pay checks of individuals; it is having deductions made from pay envelopes, it is asking people to pay in advance if they are eligible to pay. The suggestion is that the government can spend the people's money more wisely than the people themselves. There may be an argument against it, but that is our system. In recognizing the system, however, there is a

danger that with it comes altogether too much freedom in taking liberties with people's earnings, and it is my opinion we should frown upon the free and casual use of this sort of liberty by any government, regardless of its authority.
I wonder whether anyone has looked up the meaning of the word "tax". In the context of this discussion it means: "Forced contribution of wealth to meet the need of a government." Another meaning is: "A disagreeable and burdensome duty or charge." These are not very pleasant meanings for a word to have. I submit we are dealing here with something we should not be very happy about; it just happens to be a necessity that individuals shall be taxed. A noted authority has said that "the power to tax is the power to destroy". This brings into sharp focus the danger of a careless or excessive use of that power and the serious effects unlimited taxation can have upon the financial conditions of many people. It could destroy them. I am also concerned about the effect it could have upon individual initiative and effort, because it could destroy that too. It could also destroy the incentive of individuals to make full use of opportunities presented.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In the government's proposals no mention is made of governmental responsibility properly to administer and to conduct financial affairs. No mention is made of control of governmental expenditures. The government is asking the people to accept tax reforms as a responsibility of the people, but makes no mention whatever of what the government will do on behalf of the people in the disposition of tax dollars collected from them.
I submit that the white paper should not only underline the responsibility of the people to accept the principle of the collection of taxes, but it should also commit the government to undertaking a proper financial operation with proper stability by not increasing its expenditures beyond a certain percentage of the gross national product.
The proposed tax reforms have been referred to as a movement toward socialism, and other labels have been applied to them. But, surely, in any far-reaching tax reforms the government should be responsible to Parliament, and through Parliament to the people, clearly to set out the measures it proposes to adopt in the interests of the people. This policy is rendered imperative by
December 1, 1969

the inflation that exists and an apparent willingness on the part of the government to accept inflation as inevitable.
Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? In respect of the last issue of Canada Savings Bonds purchasers are guaranteed that their investment will be doubled in a period of eight years. I say this in itself is inflationary beyond question. It is probably the greatest indication of inflation today. My point is that if the government regards inflation as inevitable, it must take some measures that benefit the interests of the taxpayers, instead of merely soaking them with increased taxation. In my opinion, inflation is not inevitable. The government can cure inflation by applying business methods to meet the problem. The government is going to phase out some expenditures and live within its income. In other words, the government is going to do what Israel and West Germany have shown can be accomplished by hard work, thrift and the adoption of proper financial measures. Canada can well take a lesson from these two countries.
Since 1963 either this government or a government of the party of our friends opposite has been in office. What has been accomplished, Mr. Speaker? I should like to list some of the accomplishments. First of all, there has been an almost continuous series of deficits on ordinary account. Second, there is a degree of inflation which has brought about the highest cost of living in our history. Third, we now have the highest cost of money in history, as well as the highest expenditures. Similarly, we have had the greatest increase in taxation of any similar period in history, as well as the greatest increase in the number of bureaucrats, paid large salaries for mediocre performance, ever to be on the payroll of this country.
Deficit financing is justified only in times of high unemployment and limited economic activity. I acknowledge there have been times when this sort of situation existed and it was necessary, so to speak, to prime the pump by adopting deficit financing. However, since 1963-in fact, since 1961-all economists have agreed that we have been living in what has been termed the affluent society; times have been good. Yet successive Liberal governments have paid no attention to conditions. They have acted as though the affluent society did not exist. They have continued to borrow money and to compete with private industry. Instead of allowing private industry
Taxation Reform
to take care of capital expenditures, Liberal governments have competed with private industry for labour, for materials and for money. To a very great extent the government is responsible for the inflationary situation that now exists in Canada. The government was warned by the Governor of the Bank of Canada several years ago that this was happening, but paid no attention. Only when the situation became serious was drastic action taken.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude these remarks by reference to a capital gains tax. I feel strongly that an underdeveloped country like Canada should make a great effort to attract risk capital. Our three-year exemption from income tax and the absence of a capital gains tax attract this type of capital, the beneficial results of which have been very apparent in recent years. My leader, in the course of his speech on Friday, made our position very clear. He stated that under the government's proposals there will be less encouragement for the development of mines and of oil exploration in the more remote areas. This is undoubtedly true. The factor of capital gains caused by inflation is surely something which will be most unfair to tax in any form whatsoever.
I can understand a government proceeding with a plan to do so, but I want to refer to the suggested mechanics of applying the capital gains tax. To accept a valuation on a certain date as being final and then apply a five-year revaluation at the end of that period, regardless whether the capital gain has been realized, constitutes a tax on capital rather than a capital gains tax. I submit that a country like Canada, needing capital investment for development purposes, should not apply a tax on capital at any time. This is especially true when the rates suggested in the white paper are higher than those presently in effect in the United States. I ask the minister and the government to recognize the difference which exists, so far as tax pay-

December 1, 19S9
Taxation Reform
ments are concerned, between small business and large, widely-held business. I have some knowledge of the former because I have an association with companies which qualify under that heading.
In the first place, small companies often find it difficult to raise funds with which to pay the tax bill as rendered. In . many instances the owners are active in the management. They draw as salaries the minimum amount needed to meet living costs. They use all the available capital to effect improvements in operation by purchasing equipment, machinery, erecting buildings and making other capital expenditures designed to improve their productivity and ability to compete, sometimes with other countries for world markets. To be asked to pay in cash the capital gains tax on an accumulated basis for all their improvements in value, when their liquidity does not justify the same, leaves only one alternative; and that is to sell out, even at a price which involves a substantial sacrifice.
Then the question arises, to whom do they sell? With Canadians facing the same tax laws and having the same general limited financial resources, the prospect of their having the financial ability to purchase seems remote; so they have no choice except to sell the business, at the best price obtainable, to foreign buyers. This is a hard blow to Canadian ownership. The chances are that the buyer will be a United States company.
I have never been very worried about United States ownership of Canadian companies so long as they observe Canadian laws, if such ownership has been the determining factor in creating and developing industry. But to have tax laws which are likely to drive Canadian companies into U.S. hands through a forced sale for the reason that it may be not only be the last but perhaps the only place to go, seems most undesirable. Governments should take a very dim view of presenting such legislation.
The government must recognize the need for incentives rather than discouragement, attractive tax rates rather than the utmost in extraction, and decisions leading to growth rather than to sacrifice sales. In the language of my leader on Friday last, Canadians will regret that this government, given an opportunity to develop a tax system that would not only be more equitable but would help provide a greater opportunity for Canadians to control our economic growth, failed to do so.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if an independent
observer had listened to this debate last Friday and today, he would wonder whether the speakers were talking about the same white paper. Conservatives have described the white paper as a socialistic document and, even today, as a red manifesto, while the socialists, members of the NDP, have described it as a very conservative document.
In my opinion it is unfortunate that opposition members have taken such a partisan approach to this white paper, because when the minister introduced it he said he was putting forward proposals designed to bring about more equity in the tax system, balanced with incentives for economic growth. He said he was putting forward these proposals and wanted to hear discussion, criticisms and alternatives. However, all he got was criticism without any facts and figures behind it, and no alternatives suggested.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was speaking on Friday he said this was wrong in the white paper, and that was wrong. He criticized the increased income tax rates in the middle-income bracket; he criticized the revaluation and the five year period; he criticized other things. But he did not say how we should raise the money that we would lose if we increased exemptions at the lower level. He did not say how we would make up the $1 billion that would be lost by increasing these exemptions and adding new ones. He spoke very much as though he is in favour of everything good, and he opposes anything that is hard to take in the system. He appeared as a very lean Santa Claus in the House of Commons at this time as we approach Christmas. In his speech he almost appeared to favour motherhood.
If I could be convinced by the opposition that anything in the white paper was bad for the economy, I would certainly agree with them. However, I do not want just broad criticisms in general terms about these measures. All we have heard is wide criticism of measures. Let us know the exact dollars and cents picture behind those criticisms. If hon. members approve of the exemptions at the lower level, let them tell us how we are going to make up the money that will be lost. Such a loss has to be made up. Let them tell us in dollars and cents where that money is to be found. Let us not have this type of speech in which hon. members say they approve of the exemptions but disapprove of the increased
December 1, 1969

rates in the middle brackets and disapprove of the capital gains tax. Let us hear alternatives in specific terms. If hon. members convince me, I will vote with them.

He said "nonsense", "bunk" and then turned to another subject. I hope so. I hope we have not lost all opportunity in this debate. There will no doubt be other spokesmen and I am sure

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
That was an exception. When that system was put forward this summer, the Prime Minister said that the program to deal with bilinguahsm would be an exception. Not only that, but let me quote what the Leader of the Opposition said when these cuts were put forward by the Prime Minister. He said that it is a pretty rough kind of axe, meaning that because of this program some civil service positions would have to be eliminated. That is true; but we cannot have it both ways. You cannot restrict government spending and expect everybody to applaud. It is a tough decision to make.
Whenever we discuss the matter of restricting government expenditures, members of the opposition always want the cuts made in an area which will not affect their constituents. If you live in Montreal and are a constituent of mine, and a cut is to be made which will affect something in the city of Montreal such as the airport or harbour, you would probably say "Oh, no" and suggest that the cut should be made perhaps in respect of the Prince Edward Island causeway. I do not agree with my constituents when they say that.
Mr. Speaker, I have sat here for two days listening to hon. members opposite. I was very quiet when they spoke. I must be touching their sensitive spots now because they are becoming excited and do not appear to want to listen to me. If hon. members are really serious in suggesting to the government where cuts in spending can be made, they should be specific. They should be honest about it. If they have in mind a certain area, they should mention that area. I suggest that recommendations in respect of cuts in expenditure should not be made in a general way.

This afternoon a spokesman for the New Democratic Party stated that

they did not want any limit on the upper level. I do not know what they were suggesting. I would presume one would have to balance out the possibilities for revenue from all sources and make satisfactory decisions. It could be that it would still be possible to increase the upper level and lower the middle-income level by some figure. As I say, if a rational approach were put forward in that regard, I would accept it. I would agree with hon. members that a laudable principle is-and I would support it-that we have an equitable income tax system with graduated and progressive rates. I think this is what we should try to work out in the committee. If it can be established that it is unfair to have the levelling off on the rates of income tax at the upper levels, compared with the middle levels, let us have suggestions in respect of rates that would be workable and just.
I am quite willing to look at this question very seriously because I fully support the statement in the white paper that at present our income tax system is not equitable and that something must be done. As the minister said, we must combine incentives and economic growth with an equitable income tax system.
Although I support the general principles contained in the white paper, there are certain things I should like to see in it which are not included. I wish to mention these briefly. For example, I think that the $500 exemption for those who are 70 years old should be granted at age 65. Let us assume there are two old age pensioners, one of whom is 68 and the other 70; they each receive the old age pension, and nothing more. One would get an extra exemption because he is 70, while the other who is under 70 would not get it. I think this is an inequity, and yet it is suggested in the white paper. I believe that if there is to be an exemption for people on retirement, it should be given to all those on retirement at the age at which they receive the old age pension from the government.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Another point in the white paper with which I am not too pleased is the limit of $150 on the personal exemption in respect of people on salary. I cannot understand why a person who is working for a salary should be restricted to $150, while his colleague who may be working on his own in the same trade or profession should have no limit. I know that when I was working as a lawyer, I worked for a salary-I never worked in my
December 1, 1969

own business-and if I wanted to buy law books or buy my legal gown or the other things that are necessary for the carrying on of my profession, I received no exemption whatsoever. I had to operate under conditions which were not the same as those which applied to persons practising on their own.
Another matter in the white paper which I do not understand very clearly is the rule with respect to personal residence. I think that if we accept the premise that the personal residence should be exempt from capital gains tax, it should be exempt altogether. I cannot see the rationale behind the rule which introduces the $1,000 per year principle. I favour a system according to which the personal residence is completely exempt from capital gains tax.
Another item about which I have been concerned for several years is with respect to medical expenses. I know many people who have to buy medical supplies, such as syringes and needles for diabetics, which expense they cannot deduct under the provisions of the Income Tax Act although other people can deduct the cost of their medicines. I could never understand why a diabetic who had to buy these needles and syringes each week could not deduct their cost, just as those who had other ailments could deduct the cost of their medicines. However, there is nothing in the white paper which refers to that problem, and I would like the committee to deal with it when it meets.
There is also the question raised by paraplegics. There is a $500 exemption for people confined to a wheelchair. Originally this exemption was to help those people because they had to take taxis or pay for other means of transportation to get to work or to carry on their everyday affairs. However, the $500 exemption is out of date now. It does not in any way cover the expenses that a paraplegic or a person restricted to a wheelchair must bear. Paraplegics in my constituency have given me the exact figure, and it far exceeds $500 per year.
These are a few of the things in the white paper with which I am not too happy, and I would like the committee to deal with them if possible. There are a few other matters which have not been referred to by many people but which I think are good points which did not receive much publicity. One of them is the right to deduct gifts to national amateur athletic associations. That is a step in the right direction. It is in accord with the recommen-

dations of the task force on amateur sport. I think it will do much to stimulate the groups that are trying to promote amateur sport in this country. I think amateur sport here needs a great deal of support.
