speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to express my opinion on the white paper that was tabled.
That document, I feel, might create a very poor impression on any clever person. To describe that document, I shall use the words of Mr. Charles Neapole, president of the Montreal Stock Exchange and of the Canadian Stock Exchange, who terms that measure "nonsense". I shall base my statement on four main points.
To increase taxes by $500 million, as stated, is, I believe, a patent theft, that penalizes small enterprises, but in no way helps the consolidation of the provinces, who considers this bill with some suspicion.
I should like to deal with a point which seems to me to reflect perfectly the policy of the present government, which is proposing to tax scholarships, among other things. If I give $2 to someone and the next day I take back 50 cents, he will think surely that there is something wrong with me. Why not simply give him $1.50 instead of giving him $2 and extract from him 500 the next day. Would it be that when I gave him $2, I wanted to make a good impression or that I am not smart at figures? If I give money to a taxpayer and take back some of it the next day, it is because I am a flatterer or because I do not know how to count.
This is the position of the present government: Either the minister is not smart at figures-and this does not say very much for him-or he wants the scholarships recipients to think highly of him, even though he intends to take these grants away by way of taxes later on, and this is nothing else but false pretences.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
1 humbly suggest that this is a most realistic image of the government system as it is administered by our ministers, or as it is described in the white paper. It is nothing
1456

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
more or less than giving money to the taxpayer with one hand, either by means of scholarships, loans, allowances or anything else, and taking it back with the other, but with a smile and a flower in a button-hole.
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal now with the tax increase of $500 million. Whether this amount comes from the rich or the poor, everyone must realize, I think, that the government will take $25 more from every Canadian taxpayer. And they say that will help the Canadian people. How can the government make us understand that?
I contend that it is a patent theft as far as Canadians are concerned, and I do not believe I am the only one who thinks so, because Mr. W. H. Rapsey, former president of the Canadian manufacturers' association of electrical appliances said, and I quote:
It is patent theft.
Taxation by the government of Canada, at the stage where things are at present, is especially very contradictory and I explain myself. There are, indeed, unsold products, people condemned to unemployment, unused productive power on account of products failing to be sold and because of the lack of purchasing power, reduced for a great part by taxation. I think that all that is simply ridiculous.
Thus taxes are equal to theft nowadays because they should exist but only to take surplus money out of circulation while there are too few products. When money is needed, taxes should not be levied but purchasing power should be distributed through the grant of a national dividend and a compensatory discount, which would bring prices down to the real cost of production.
The financing of governments, of public investments must be made through new credits according to the actual needs and the production capacity of Canada, not through a tax increase at the expense of producers. Which brings me to tell the house that small businesses will therefore be the most hardly hit by the proposed reforms.
We are back where we started. Indeed, a year ago, the Post Office DeDartment curiously strangled a good deal of small publishing businesses, under the pretext of serving the interests of the Department which, I insist, must serve the Canadian people; the opposite should not be true.
Now, I would like to quote an article of Mr. Fraser Robertson published in the Globe and Mail of November 12, in which he noted how

contemptuous of small businesses the government seems to be, according to the contents of the white paper. Here is what he said:
In his proposals he chose to term a tax reform, the Minister of Finance obviously endorses the views of the Economic Council of Canada, namely that what Canada needs is the development of a few powerful monopolies which could easily fall under the responsibility of other cabinet members. He scorns small businesses, especially family ventures, thus reflecting the arrogance of our times.
Recalling that big companies such as General Motors, IBM and Massey Ferguson had modest beginnings, that they were small concerns before becoming powerful monopolies, Mr. Robertson said that even now, big businesses must rely on the small ones to obtain the raw materials they need.
He recalls that General Electric, for example, has more than 10,000 small suppliers.
By stifling small concerns, we must not forget that the government will be hurting the monopolies and will not encourage the Canadian economy. Those proposals are therefore contrary to those which should be set forth in the white paper.
Mr. Speaker, should a capital gains tax be levied, private industrial investments are going to be curtailed and the people's consuming power is going to be greatly reduced.
As a matter of fact, if capital gains are taxed, foreign and even Canadian businessmen will not be interested any longer in investing in our country. As a result, the productive sector which is kept rolling by investments-you will agree with me on that point-will be greatly paralyzed, hence unemployment, our natural resources left unused and high prices for our products. In a word, it will be a big setback in every field of our country's economy, even though our country is regarded as highly industrialized.
I believe that the fiscal reform proposals, if adopted as they are, will demonstrate an approach both ultra-conservative and ultrareactionary since studies carried out by top economists have established that the government should use the budget to carry out a fiscal policy over an economic cycle in order to maintain current production at a level as close as possible to that of potential full-employment and maximum production and to balance the budget from year to year, a policy followed by the governments before the 1929-1930 economic slump.
It seems to me that the government does not follow a functional, modern financial policy, which would centre on the means to
December 1. 1969

have an economy of full employment while avoiding unwarranted price increases.
For this reason I think that the government, in submitting its white paper, is acting contrary to all modern principles of government. I suggest that the Minister of Finance should consult other competent economists so that he can present tax measures designed to ensure the progress of our economy and not its regression.
In an article published last Saturday in La Presse, Mr. Paul Allard, Minister of Natural Resources in Quebec, wonders seriously about the federal proposal to tax capital gains and to modify the tax rates, and I quote:
Speaking at the Universal Motel in Quebec, Mr. Allard stated that a certain danger might result from such policies, that "investors might prefer putting aside some no doubt productive but somewhat risky investments and concentrate on those offering higher dividends."
"Such a reaction" Mr. Allard added, "may have disastrous effects on the opening of new industries especially with regard to natural resources. It would be too bad if, through some action designed to give a more equitable tax system, the government should cause a slowing-down of the economy and as a consequence an increase in unemployment and in the cost of living."
I believe that federal-provincial relations are truly in need of a catalytic agent in order to develop in a peaceful climate.
The white paper on taxation, far from promoting understanding, is rather another vexatious measure imposed on the provinces by the federal government.
In British Columbia, Mr. Dan Campbell, Minister of Municipal Affairs, indicated that this document does not mention at all the provincial or municipal authorities whose views must, of course, be taken into consideration in any fiscal reform.
Premier Harry Strom of Alberta, in conjunction with other politicians in that province, regrets that nothing is done to alleviate the tax burden of the provinces and the municipalities in his own province.
Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland fears that the capital gains tax will jeopardize capital investments in Canadian industry.
In closing, I wish to tell the House that a tax reform is a good thing in itself provided it is not negative and does not interfere with the eoonomy, since it is a pyramid in which the biggest businesses depend on the smallest ones, while the smallest ones depend on the individual.
Now, if the government strangles the small businesses, the big consortiums will be in a bad predicament and this tax reform will be

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF WHITE PAPER ON TAXATION REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the document we are discussing is misnamed a white paper. In reality it is a murky grey. It is as difficult to see its real purpose and to judge its actual impact as it is to see the outlines of anything in a heavy fog. The economic objectives of a democratic society in which the greater part of economic activity is managed by free enterprise are generally considered to be as follows: full employment, reasonable price stability and a satisfactory balance of payments, all combined with an adequate rate of economic growth. The white paper proposals must be judged by their efficacy in fostering these goals. The position of the people who drafted the white paper on taxation is that Canadian national identity is so fragile that if outside economic influences are not restricted by using government action, the absorption of Canada will inevitably take place. By implication, anything Canadian per se is valuable, and outsiders less valuable. The white paper proposes many measures to foster this point of view.
To begin with, it is questionable whether these proposals will produce the benefits to the Canadian people that are claimed for them. They are more likely to have the effect of countervailing action or, at best, benefiting particular groups of Canadians at the national expense. The arguments that have been trotted out are the customary old fallacies: inability to compete with foreigners in free competition demonstrates their superior potential efficiency lurking beneath the surface, so that a subsidy of one kind or another is justified.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in explaining the aims of his tax reform proposals, said they were to attain a more equitable application of the tax burden, to maintain prosperity and steady economic growth. An examination of the white paper indicates to me that not only will its provisions not attain these objectives, but they are more likely to achieve results diametrically opposed. The minister proposes to take away any trace of a tax burden from a large segment of low-income Canadians, lighten it considerably in respect of Canadians who enjoy very high

December 1, 1969
Taxation. Reform
incomes, and sock it to the middle-income group. This is a deceptively simple explanation, and when coupled with the claim of greater equality it is somewhat dishonest.
The group he plans to sock it to are the very people who are currently carrying the greatest share of Canada's total tax burden. They are, largely, the creators and the doers, the producers of national wealth and development. They are also the same group that pays for education through municipal property taxes, and for soaring costs of higher education and welfare and health programs through provincial taxes of one type oi another. There is a real danger here of the minister killing the geese that lay the golden eggs.
Lower income groups would be helped by raising the annual exemptions, for single taxpayers from $1,000 to $1,400 and for married taxpayers from $2,000 to $2,800. If both parents are working, an exemption of $500 per child is provided for costs connected with the outside supervision of children. Of the estimated 7,700,000 taxpayers, theoretically 750,000 would be removed from the tax rolls. This contrasts with the widely accepted theory that everyone should file a tax return and pay some tax even if it is a nominal one only, so that he realizes he is part of the community and not just a guest here. Taxes for about 3,000,000 would supposedly be reduced slightly, but the burden of taxes would be shifted to those who earn more than $9,100 per year, hypothetically 3,000,000 other taxpayers. On the other hand, the maximum tax rate would be lowered from 80 per cent to 50 per cent, but this would not affect very many because few taxpayers actually pay more than 50 per cent over-all, even under the existing schedules.
Income redistribution to favour lower income categories would be of some assistance to handicapped people who cannot function effectively. Tax relief to lower paid Canadians in some measure helps those who are starting their working careers and whose small incomes do not reflect their actual conditions. It would have been more fruitful to recognize the social needs of the disadvantaged in other ways. For example, the government could permit voluntary workers and teachers to include the cost of the time they spend in assisting the handicapped. Advisory work, employment counselling and voluntary teaching could have been given a boost if the time spent by volunteers were allowed to count as a tax reduction for these workers, at [Mr. Ritchie.1
reasonable rates. Also, professional advisory training and job counselling firms specifically geared to help the handicapped should have been given tax considerations as an effective way of encouraging the private sector to participate in the effort needed to alleviate distress.
The estimates of the number of taxpayers who would be aided and/or hurt by the income redistribution proposals were based on 1967 figures. Inasmuch as wage gains have been averaging about 8 per cent per year compounded, by 1972 the number of taxpayers in the middle-income bracket would be nearer 4,500,000, not 3,000,000 which is assumed by the white paper. Middle-income taxpayers would bear the brunt of the tax increases proposed by the government. Similarly, the number who would gain from the revisions would be less than the white paper estimates and fewer than 750,000 would be dropped from the tax rolls.
The white paper is more of a social and political document than an economic one. No doubt there is a rich harvest of votes to be had by anyone who can remove 750,000 people from taxation. No doubt the proposals suggested will help to get this government off the hook of the overambitious and vastly expensive social welfare programs it plans to launch or has already launched. But the real problems of Canada have been deliberately avoided and sacrificed to political popularity and expediency.
The Economic Council of Canada emphasized what was already very clear, that each year this country must create thousands and thousands of new jobs simply to keep our economy turning over at the same pace, let alone speeding it up. Yet the reforms suggested in the white paper will sorely cripple, if not kill, the business expansion, the new economic initiative and the spirit of development vitally necessary to create these needed jobs. "The word 'reform' is an euphemism for increasing taxes", a leading Manitoba tax expert, 1. H. Asper, said in a recent speech about the white paper. Even increased taxes might be supportable if it were certain that the new taxes would go for positive, productive development programs and not simply to carry Canada's multitude of ill-conceived, badly constructed and foolishly expensive social welfare schemes.
This, of course, brings us to another major weakness of the tax reforms suggested, the failure to consult about them with the prov-
December 1, 1969



inces, the failure to take the growing crisis in federal-provincial tax and financial relations into account and above all, the disastrous effect the tax reforms will have upon our already grievous regional disparity.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that one of our most grave economic complaints, one that intimately affects the federal and provincial governments' need for more tax revenue and their inability to undertake many much needed development programs, is the unbusinesslike manner in which our major social welfare programs operate. Take any of them, medicare, hospitalization, and so on; they all appear to operate without even the most primitive form of cost control. The result is that all levels of government in Canada today are caught in a vortex of rapidly accelerating costs which they do not seem to know how to check or control. It is little wonder that people like the Minister of Finance will attempt any subterfuge, underwrite any wild scheme, to procure the great quantity of tax revenue needed every year by these open-ended programs that apparently cannot be changed and certainly cannot be abolished.
As to regional disparity, many provinces, including my own province of Manitoba, suffer from several severe economic handicaps. They are discriminated against in such matters as tariffs, freight rates, immigration policy, regional development and half a hundred other areas. What they all desperately need-in fact, it is a common No. 1 priority- is industrial growth; and it is industrial growth that suffers most from the tax reforms suggested in the white paper. They actually penalize small business, individual initiative and enterprise. These factors are the whole foundation of industrial development and expansion.
New tax rates on business also would affect middle-income groups in other ways. The existing 21 per cent tax rate on small business is raised to 50 per cent, whether it is paid out in dividends or in gains in selling shares in these "closely held" businesses. This hurts family-controlled concerns and other small establishments. It is detrimental to growing enterprises. The natural urge to plough back earnings for growth expansion is squelched, and growth is thus diminished. Therefore, it would encourage small business to sell its shares to the public as widely-held Canadian shares listed on exchanges and becoming subject to the lower 25 per cent capital gains tax.
Taxation Reform
Dividends received from Canadian corporations would entail a credit equal to the tax paid by the corporation. Thus, if a Canadian corporation paying 50 per cent tax to the federal government declared a dividend of $1 per share, the recipient would "gross up" his dividend to $1 plus the 50 per cent rate of taxation, or $1.50 per share, and the shareholder would receive a credit of 50 cents per share in respect of his own tax. This is the main and only true sweetener for investors and would replace the present 20 per cent dividend tax credit. This would be a discrimination against those holding bonds and mortgages, because until the taxpayer reached an income of approximately $17,000 it would be greatly to their advantage to have shares in widely-held Canadian corporations and not hold mortgage or bond issues.
Pension funds would be obligated to have at least 90 per cent of their assets in Canadian investments or they would be subject to tax. This would replace the present requirement that only 10 per cent of the income of pension funds could be derived from nonCanadian sources. There is an assumption here that the primary obligation of pension funds is not to ensure maximum safety for the pension fund recipients at the least cost to the contributors; rather, it is suggested that pension funds should invest in things Canadian regardless of their relative merit.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Income from non-Canadian sources would be penalized so that Massey Ferguson, Moore Corporation or a distillery company would not be entitled to pass on a dividend credit to their Canadian share-holders on taxes paid outside Canada. International companies such as these would be discouraged, therefore, from locating their headquarters in Canada!
Similarly, subsidiaries abroad would be discouraged. Interest charges incurred as part of the debt structure of these subsidiaries would not be allowed, and the low rate of taxes of such subsidiaries would be discontinued. In many cases firms establish subsidiaries abroad in underdeveloped areas where they receive a several-year tax exemption from the host country; but now these tax-free earnings will be taxed by Canada. Consulting firms, among others, would no longer be likely to set up a foreign subsidiary in these havens. This would tend to discourage Canadian exports, because consulting firms and other subsidiaries usually promote the use of products and equipment with which they are familiar.

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
Any analysis of the white paper must take note of the careless anomalies which are present. For example, Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, E.I. duPont, Ford, Union Carbide and others would be obligated to pay every five years a tax of 25 per cent of the "paper" gains in the value of their Canadian subsidiaries based on market price changes of their stock. The five-year assessment of unrealized gains could not work for individual shareholders of many Canadian stocks classified as widely-held, because of the limited marketability of many issues. There are innumerable other examples which illustrate the impractical nature of the proposed legislation. There is no point in dwelling on this aspect of the white paper except to state that the improper drafting will inevitably mean that many of the proposals will have to be redrawn, even in the unlikely event that the basic concepts were accepted by the nation.
The onerous nature of many of these proposals, some apparently serving no purpose other than sheer maliciousness, such as the arbitrary periodic taxation of gains whether realized or not, will encourage tax evasion on an unprecedented scale in Canada. Enforcement, after all, depends ultimately on the consent of the taxed. The valuation of personal property, improvements of houses or farms and taxing gains in foreign securities would be so difficult to police that tax avoidance would become commonplace.
Without industrial and commercial growth there can be no new profits to tax, no new salaries to tax and no accumulated capital either to employ or to tax. If this growth slows because of discriminatory taxation or for any other reason, if it begins to dwindle, then so will tax revenues and the standard of life. If we ever allow this to happen we are simply creating for ourselves more non-productive social deadweight that will require a great expenditures of tax money to carry. This is why, in my estimation, the tax proposals as they now stand are so short-sighted and so damaging.
Capital, business ability and imagination always seek a congenial atmosphere. They take freight easily and move away swiftly. There is nothing in this proposal for tax reform that is congenial to capital or business, and in many respects it is freightening. At the very time we Canadians should be bending all our efforts to encouraging capital and business enterprise and know-how at home, we are by this white paper threatening them. If you doubt, as the minister professes

to doubt, that individuals or small businesses will pull up stakes, let me give one or two examples. Take the case of a man in Winnipeg earning about $13,000 annually, smack in the middle of the group the minister has threatened to soak. In some instances under the new tax proposals he would pay $3,100 in tax, while a man with the same salary across the United States border in Minneapolis would pay only about $1,100. There is the example of a Winnipeg company manufacturing a certain product which it sells 90 per cent of in the United States. If he moved his business to Minneapolis, the proprietor of that small business would increase his after-tax profit by 50 per cent strictly on the basis of differences in the tax systems.
All one needs to do is look at the Dominion Bureau of Statistics' figures regarding the natural population increase in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Manitoba's population increased naturally by 70,000 during the years quoted in the figures, and Saskatchewan's population increased naturally by 75,000. But with a net migration for Manitoba of 28,000 and for Saskatchewan 45,000, Manitoba was left with an actual increase in population of only 41,000, and Saskatchewan 30,000. Canada must stop the haemorrhage that is bleeding us of brains, capital and know-how. These proposed reforms will only quicken the bleeding.
I mentioned the murky look of this white paper and the difficulty of seeing clearly what it intended. There are many who see much greater dangers in it than any I have mentioned. A highly respected Montreal financial and investment firm, Jones Heward and Company, were quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press as saying in part:
The white paper is no simple Robin Hood approach to society, no simple accountant's concept of a redistribution of income, but a pure and simple attack on the free enterprise system embodying a punitive and discriminatory capital gains tax, a capital levy every five years, and an increased tax burden on the middle income productive group of Canada. There is no room for the small business with enterprise and imagination.
The same firm stated that "wealth is to be destroyed". Surely, Mr. Speaker, when such things can be said by responsible and knowledgeable Canadian firms, it behooves us all to take the closest look at the subject of the charge. After all, the cardinal tenet of Marxism is the destruction of private wealth. Other reputable authorities have made similar grave charges and have seen in this white paper, not a makeshift economic program but
December 1, 1969

an extremely radical blueprint for social and political change.
The assumptions of the white paper are that the government needs more revenue because more than $1 billion would be collected if the scheme were fully operating, given present levels of the economy. There is no mention of the fact that taxes can or should be used for economic stabilization or growth. Little consideration is paid to the implication of these tax levels on the economy, incentives for work or capital accumulation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how often a participant in a debate in this House begins by outlining those things which he proposes to avoid. Perhaps unlike the speakers who contributed to this debate last Friday and today, I do not intend to deal specifically with the widsom or otherwise of releasing some of the tax burden from the low-income people, although in my constituency there is a very heavy preponderance of people who carry a lunch-pail and punch the clock. It was welcome news that the government intended to alleviate the tax burden on that taxpayer.
I will not comment on the wisdom or otherwise of increasing the tax rates for those people whose incomes fall in the $10,000 to $30,000 bracket, nor will I talk about the crack-down on expense account living. I will not comment on the capital gains tax, although it certainly has a very direct effect on my constituency. Nor will I talk about the wisdom or otherwise of changing the situation with respect to the mining industry and the tax holidays they have enjoyed in the past.
The reason that I am not going to deal specifically with subjects of that sort, Mr. Speaker, is that I think they are matters of individual taxation approach and are not so much a question of the broad philosophical concern that we should be dealing with at this time. In any case, even if it were a proper consideration to be debated in this chamber, I would draw attention to the fact
Taxation Reform
that when the white paper on taxation policy is about to be transferred from this chamber to the standing committee, is not the time to be dealing with these specific items, the specific concerns of pages 1, 2, 3, 20 or 30 of the white paper.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
This is, in my opinion, the time for us to concern ourselves with a more philosophical approach. I suppose hon. members who have had more experience in this chamber than I will be somewhat surprised to find someone standing up and talking about the philosophy of government or the basic principles of government in a democratic society, of government for the people, of the people, by the people, or whatever combination of those words one wants to use at any given time.
Some of these phrases may sound a little tired, or as if they came from an essay by a political science student. Nevertheless, I think it is an appropriate time for us to consider the basic philosophic principles underlying our system of government. I say this because today, perhaps more than at any time in the history of our country, we are aware of the influences which are attempting to divide us as Canadian citizens, to set provincial governments against the federal government, province against province, east against west, citizens of one linguistic group against those of another. These forces are stronger now than at any time in our history.
When we talk about separatism, or the tendency to try to divide us and break up our institutions, we are not taken as lightly as we were a few years ago. Of course, it is not radical to talk about the fact that there are forces at work in this nation today which would divide us and break up confederation. But the ideological forces which compare our system of government with the systems in vogue in other countries are no longer distant, no longer theoretical. They are present in our country today, taking their place and making their influence felt. It is no accident that people are talking about separatist influences and subversive influences in everyday speech in this country.
When people in various parts of our nation are talking in these terms and, particularly, when the young people in our schools and universities are telling us that our political system is out of step and irrelevant, it is surely time for us to become concerned. When they come to us, as they came to the

December 1, 1969
Taxation Reform
recent convention of our party, not to tell us, not that they support some other political party, or that our party is not as good as one of the other opposition parties, but to tell us that all our parties are irrelevant to the needs of the Canadian people today, we had better wake up and consider whether our system of government can stand up to this kind of scrutiny.
I think this is an appropriate time at which to consider whether the approach we are taking to the subject of taxation in this white paper is, from all points of view, the correct one, the democratic one, so that regardless of our individual political differences, regardless of the narrower approach which individual hon. members may take, we can all of us in the long run say we are proud of the system we employ to govern ourselves and that we believe it will stand up to the scrutiny and attacks of those in our country who deride and denigrate it, try to separate us and break down confederation rather than support it.
When we examine our system of taxation as a whole we realise we are not dealing with a piece of legislation which affects one part of the country; we are not dealing with a piece of legislation which has to do with a particular region or a particular pressure group; we are not dealing with legislation which concerns one particular facet of Canadian life; we are dealing with something which touches every citizen of every age, in every walk of life. Thus it is appropriate to ask ourselves whether our handling of this important and comprehensive subject is consistent with our understanding of good democracy and representative government. It involves the power of the government to collect money, and this in turn influences directly its ability to continue its programs or embark on new ones, to spend money, much of which will be redistributed among our citizens. It affects every citizen, every possibility, every potential, every hope which Canadians have for the future. More important still, it represents our approach in 1969 to the correct government policy involved in the redistribution of the wealth of this nation. If this is not sufficiently important from the point of view of every taxpayer, I cannot imagine what is.
If there is one area in which the federal government must take a lead at this time, if there is one clear, consistent and strong reason for supporting the federalist type of governmental system in this country, it is the necessity for a central government able to assume primary responsibility for redistribut-

ing money to the citizens among the economic groups of all the regions. The federal government must see to it that the power to collect taxes and the consequent power to spend money is used in such a way as to promote economic equality. So we are testing the very fabric of the government, which involves the right to tax and the method of doing so.
We are testing its programs and its ability to take money and spend it among the less privileged of our nation; we are examining the role of the government in redistributing the wealth of our nation. The final test of any governmental system is: to what extent does it see to it, through our system of taxation and spending, that all citizens have a reasonable opportunity to enjoy a decent standard of living? In doing this, we are examining what I believe to be the very basis of our system of government. In this respect we should take pride in the fact that we have advanced to a stage at which we can abandon the archaic system under which changes in taxation policy could only be implemented under conditions of the greatest secrecy and could only be enforced by means of a budget which was kept secret even from members of this House until it was announced. Measures thus introduced take effect with stunning force and the citizens directly concerned wake up to find themselves suddenly confronted by news of the way in which the government proposes to collect money from certain sources for redistribution to others.
This atmosphere of secrecy was, in my opinion, a weakness in our system of government. The fact we have now progressed to a stage at which we are able to adopt a white paper approach, and table in this House complete background information outlining in detail the policy of the government on taxation matters, is something which I profoundly welcome. This gives the nation an opportunity to react, an opportunity to understand the background and to express its views, an opportunity for citizens to discuss the measures proposed and apply them to their own way of life, to their own spheres of activity, to their own line of work or class of business. This in turn enables them to take part in our democratic and representative way of government by voicing their reactions.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
In addition, I take pride in the fact that we will also be using extensively the facilities of the standing committees' system. When this debate is concluded the matter will be trans-
December 1. 1969

ferred to a standing committee. In line with the rules changes recently made in this chamber and the increased responsibilities given to our standing committees, a full discussion and detailed examination of this document will there take place. All members of the chamber will have an opportunity to question those responsible for this white paper, to examine the government officials involved and, more importantly, to bring to the floor of the standing committee the views of their constituents as to the wisdom or otherwise of every page and paragraph, every proposal and provision contained in this white paper on taxation policy.
This is an important debate because we are discussing for the first time the white paper approach to a comprehensive taxation policy for Canada. When the matter is put on the floor of the standing committee for extensive and detailed study, we will be able to test our system of government further, and in two ways, the first being the capacity of every citizen in his country to voice his reaction to this important policy.
Since the introduction of this document I have spent a number of hours on week ends in my own constituency talking with various people about the white paper. Certainly it adds nothing new to this debate to put on record that the people at the lower end of the income scale are, generally speaking, happy at the fact that their tax burden will be lessened if these proposals are implemented. Neither is it surprising, I am sure, to inform the House that the people who are expressing greatest concern at the present time are those businessmen and others whose incomes fall within the $10,000 to $30,000 or $35,000 bracket.
Over the past weekend I discussed at great length these proposals with what I consider to be a good cross-section of my community. For example, I talked with the operator of a dry cleaning business, with the operator of a refrigeration business, with an architect, an accountant and the regional sales manager of a very large manufacturing concern. Each of these persons expressed different concerns and problems that he felt he would meet if these proposals were introduced.
With regard to the crackdown on expense account living, the feeling was that although others were able to advertise and charge the cost as an operating expense, under the new proposals they would be unable to take advantage of tax exemptions on money spent
Taxation Reform
entertaining clients personally. However, such details are not the important matter; what concerns me is the opportunity that each of these persons, in his own individual capacity, will have to make a forceful representation to this House in regard to the problems he will face if these proposals are introduced.
All members of this House-not simply government members, or opposition members in their narrow political capacities, but all members-are faced with a challenge, and it is this: Are they going to use the views of their constituents to their own political advantage, or are they prepared to make a full contribution to the representative and democratic process that is involved in examining that most important facet of government, the power by taxation to raise and to spend money?
I suggest we face not one but two challenges. First of all, by being responsible members of this House we have to assist each individual citizen to react to this white paper. In addition to that, through our work on standing committees and in our contributions to this debate, both before and after the subject is studied in the standing committee, we must see to it that this chamber possesses the capacity to evaluate public reaction and apply it to government policy.
If we are successful, then in the final analysis, when these proposals are implemented in a year or 14 months from now, we will be secure in the knowledge that the white paper has had the best possible exposure to the democratic and representative process of government. Whatever be the final policy of the government, we will be able to say with pride that it has resulted from good democratic, representative government in Canada today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last act was rather difficult to follow. The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has made the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) look like someone a little left of Karl Marx. My following the hon. member for Crowfoot will, I hope, put him back in some kind of perspective, perhaps not so far as the twentieth century but possibly so far as the late nineteenth century is concerned.
The white paper has been proclaimed by many members on the government side, including the Minister of Finance, as a great, progressive document. However, if our standard of comparison is taxation policies in advanced industrial nations, including those in western Europe, the document is in fact a conservative one. Considered in the light of progress, the document is very long on suggestion and very short on substance. One of the best signs that this document is a conservative proposal in Canada is the fact that most newspapers in the country have accepted the general principles outlined in it. When editorial writers in Canada's newspapers accept something, it is a pretty good indication that we are not in for a radical change.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The government members have made a lot of the fact that 750,000 people are going to be taken off the tax list. I for one am not at all impressed by this fact, if one looks at what will be the average tax saving. A man who saves $20, $30, $100 or even $200 in taxes, according to the proposal which, if we are lucky, will be implemented two years hence, will have that very quickly written off, given the trend of inflation in this country. So the gains are really insubstantial, I suggest.
What are the principles of good government spending and of a just taxation system? I suggest they are four: first, taxes should be based on ability to pay; second, tax proposals

should be comprehensive, that is to say, all income should be included-a buck is a buck, as many have said; third, the tax system in an advanced country should have, as one of its principal objectives, the goal of achieving a redistribution of incomes; fourth, the tax system, in the judgment of this party, should be one means of offsetting the influence of a consumer goods industry by providing needed public goods and services such as hospitals, parks, athletic facilities, theatres, streets, schools and universities.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) last Friday in this debate tried to deal in a general way with each of these objectives. I would like to take the time available to me to deal with one in particular, that is, the argument that has been advanced by the New Democratic Party that even if implemented-and we have no guarantee of this- the proposals for tax reform in the white paper would still leave Canada with a taxation system which grossly favours the rich as opposed to the average and the poor income people.
I want to try to document this argument very briefly. First of all, nothing would be done about the serious plight of the poor in this country. The Economic Council of Canada showed that the percentage of income of low-income people in this country, of people at the poverty level in fact, has not changed in a significant way in the last couple of decades. It has also been shown by the Economic Council of Canada that the percentage of income of the bottom 20 per cent of families in the income schedule of this country between 1951 and 1965 did not change. In 1951, 20 per cent of families on the income scale received only 6.1 per cent of income. In 1965, some 14 years later, this increased to 6.7 per cent, or almost no change. The second 20 per cent rose only from 12.9 per cent to 13.4 per cent in the same period. In 1965, just four years ago, the bottom 40 per cent of Canadian families received only 20 per cent of the income.
What is the conclusion? The conclusion, also very ably documented in a whole series of studies that have appeared in recent years, is that 20 per cent of Canadians live in poverty-serious, unhealthy, unpleasant poverty. They consist of the elderly, the people in our rural areas, probably half the population of the Atlantic provinces, a large number in Quebec, a very high percentage of our Indian and Metis population, and many thousands in the cores of our large cities. Another 20 per
[Mr. Broadbent.l
cent of the population are barely above the level of poverty. What does this mean? It means that 40 per cent of Canadians, almost half the population, live on very low incomes.
What does the white paper really propose to do about this situation? One suggestion has been to raise the exemption to $1,400 and to $2,800 for married couples. Will this lift the burden of taxes completely from the poor? No, it will not. According to the Economic Council of Canada, even in 1967 a family with two children needed a minimum income of $4,200 to get by. In his speech last Friday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) indicated he knew very well that many of Canada's poor would still be paying taxes if this white paper is accepted.
He accepted the fact then-and I think it bears repetition-that this great document proposing a taxation reform will still leave thousands of Canadian families living in a state of poverty and paying taxes. He indicated in the debate on Friday that to change this we would have to increase taxes on the rich to levels beyond the one which he is proposing. I say: Why not increase the level of taxation well beyond what is proposed here for those who can afford to pay? Why not remove completely the special tax exemptions which still remain for the petroleum industry and others? If we take seriously the goal of eradicating poverty, as have countries with a per capita income much lower than our own, we can do it; but it means those who are in a position to do so will have to pay more taxes.
A few years ago I spent a month in Scandinavia, a good part of that time in Norway. When I was there in 1963 the per capita income was approximately the same as that in Great Britain, but the distribution of income was very different. I was given to understand at the time that only some 1,100 people in that country had incomes which exceeded $10,000 a year. But the social effects were amazing. Nowhere in that country did I see concentrations of poverty. Nowhere did I see grotesquely run-down cities or undernourished and badly-clothed children. The reason is simple. Given the same per capita income as Great Britain, which is much lower than that in our country, their government was seriously concerned with the problem of poverty and applied taxation as a means of social reform. In order to look after those who needed it, they taxed those who could afford to pay.

[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It is a shame to suggest that this document before us moves in any significant degree in that direction, and I am astounded by my friends on the political right, and also those on my physical right in this House, who rise and suggest we have here a radical document of some sort. That is absurd. Not only is there no significant increase in the tax levels for the higher income groups, but the whole means of taxing and the degree to which the rate is raised seem to me to be basically erroneous. Raising the exemption level, as has been pointed out, is in fact benefiting those at the higher levels in terms of dollars. It benefits them more than the poor. What should have been used in much greater degree is a whole series of tax credits, and these could have been applied to the lower levels only.
The answer is a complete system of tax credits instead of exemptions. As calculated by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) in his speech on Friday last, such a system would raise two-thirds of the money which the minister's proposals are designed to raise. The second and related point to be made is that the wealthy in Canada are quite happy. In the Minister of Finance we do not have a Robin Hood, a man who takes from the very rich and gives to the very poor.
What are the real facts about the increases in taxation? A married couple, with two children, who have an income of $20,000 will pay only $60 more. If such a married man earns $25,000 he will pay only $47 more, and if he should be a poor man with an income of $30,000 he will pay only $35 more. On the very highest level of income, Mr. Speaker, the government, this supposedly progressive government, has the audacity to put a 51 per cent ceiling on income tax. What view of justice, I ask, can lead the government to tax men living in the state of poverty in Canada, but allow millionaires to have a 51 per cent tax ceiling? Anyone who would suggest that this is at all just needs to undergo very serious self-analysis.
The principle is clear. With this proposal, the richer you are in Canada the smaller is your tax increase. It is no excuse to say, "Oh yes, but we are also going to tax those people on capital gains. They have not been taxed that way before." That is a curious kind of fallacious argument. Because we perpetrated an injustice for many years by not taxing capital gains, the government now says we should modify the blow by taxing them at a very modest rate. This is an argument of the most expedient political kind. It says to the
Taxation Reform
higher income group who vote for the Liberal Party, "Don't switch back to the Conservatives now. We are not going to be too tough on you. We are not going to introduce a really just system of taxation."
Generally speaking, as has been pointed out the real burden of increases in taxation is to be felt by those with incomes between $9,000 and $15,000. Why not on the rich? Why the special exemptions for certain kinds of industries? Why not a higher increase in corporation taxes? If we want to remove poverty and lift the burden of taxes that will still be paid by people living in poverty, why do we not do those things?
I would now like to turn to another example of inequity in the proposed system. It concerns the supposed benefit that an employed person can obtain by deducting certain expenses for his work. A $150 ceiling has been placed on the amount a worker can claim. Why this ceiling? Why impose such a limit on what a working man can claim when no equivalent limit is placed on employers or professional people? Again, it appears a clear case of discrimination which favours the rich over the poor. It is very hard for me to escape the conclusion that there is a very high degree of cynicism involved. To me it is an unscrupulous trick, the main purpose of which is to get the working people to accept the higher rates of deductions allowed for other people.
The fourth point I want to make on this general question of benefits which favour the rich over the poor and the average Canadian, concerns the failure of the government to embark upon a serious program of public investment and public expansion. If we build public swimming pools, parks and universities, the average income and poor Canadian benefits as much as the rich. If we remove pollution from our waters and air, if we preserve and build attractive cities, if we expand our hospitals and increase our medical research, the ordinary Canadian gains as much as his wealthy neighbour.
All of these are public goods; all require public investment. They all tend to favour the ordinary or the average man with benefits he could not purchase on the open market. Through this kind of use of our economic resources we can really equalize conditions to a very significant degree for all Canadians. However, if we look at the white paper we again see the kind of discrimination which tends to perpetuate the status quo as against expansion in this public domain.

Mr. Speaker, on November 20 I addressed the following question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), as recorded at page 1031 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce whether his department is investigating the charge made by the Canadian director of the United Auto Workers that the Ford Maverick car produced at St. Thomas and exported to the United States is sold there for $380 less than in Canada?
The minister was not very impressed with my question or with the importance of the problem, because his answer consisted of simply saying:
These things happen. It is quite possible that a company's general marketing policies give rise to this situation.
In other words, the minister saw nothing wrong with the policy and proposed to do nothing about it. It is interesting that the minister thought there was nothing wrong and proposed to do nothing about a policy under which Canadians will pay more for a product produced in Canada and exported to the United States.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
On the same day the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) was asked whether, in view of the increased prices for natural gas being paid in the United States which would undoubtedly lead to an increased price in Canada for natural gas, he would consider a policy whereby prices in Canada would be less than those in the United States. The minister suggested that it was an inefficient industry which permitted a two-price system, one in Canada and one in the United States. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is inefficient in the opinion of Liberal ministers if the price paid in Canada is less than the price paid in the United States, but it is quite normal if Canadians pay more for something produced in Canada which sells for less in the United States.
What are the facts in this case? There are two Ford plants, one at St. Thomas in Ontario and one at Kansas City, which produce all Ford "Mavericks" being made. Seventy-five per cent of the Ford "Mavericks" produced at the St. Thomas plant are exported to the United States and sold there. What do we find? These cars are shipped across the border every day, duty free. The same type of car off the same assembly line, built by the same workers with the same materials and the same built-in cost factor sells for $380 less in the United States than in Canada. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the minute the car crosses the border the price is reduced by $380. Part of that differential is due to the different tax system, but according to the company the remainder of it is due to the fact that warranty servicing is more expensive in Canada, Canadians roads are more expensive and the policy of bilingualism is adding to the Canadian price.
These are merely excuses. When we dealt with the U.S.-Canada auto pact we were told that a number of things would happen: We would produce more cars in Canada, and this has happened; we would reduce the balance of trade deficit as a result of auto transactions, which was important and has happened. We were also told that part of the cost to the Canadian taxpayer would be that we could no longer collect $50 in duty because that, in effect, now goes to the automobile companies; that the industry would be more efficient; that it would be rationalized for production; that runs would be longer and therefore prices would come down. But that has not happened. As I have pointed out, in the case of the "Maverick", prices are substantially higher in Canada than in the United

States. The price of cars produced in Canada is higher in Canada than that of the same cars shipped to the United States.
There are two explanations for this, Mr. Speaker. Either every car shipped to the United States and sold for less than in Canada is sold at a loss-and I do not believe that, nor do I believe that the minister or his parliamentary secretary would argue that-or the price in Canada is such that the companies are making an exorbitant profit on Canadian sales. I suggest that the minister could handle this situation either by renegotiating the U.S.-Canada auto pact or by removing the duty, so that if the individual consumer wants to purchase a car he can bring it in duty free in the same way as Ford, General Motors or Chrysler. The day he can do that, Mr. Speaker, there will be real competition and the price will come down to where it ought to be.

Mr. Speaker, because of the unavoidable absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and his parliamentary secretary, I shall be pleased to reply to the hon. member's questions.
It was indicated in the House previously that the suggested retail price of the Ford "Maverick" is United States $1995 for sales in the United States, and Canada $2375 for sales in Canada. After making allowances for exchange and the higher federal sales tax in Canada, and allowing for the effect of dealer mark-up, a difference of about $100 in Canadian funds or 5 per cent remains. In looking at this residual difference of about $100 or 5 per cent, I think I can do no better than quote from a paragraph at page 10588 of Hansard for June 25, 1969, where the parliamentary secretary to the minister made an answer to a very similar question concerning the price differential of the "Maverick". I quote it because I think it is a very fair statement of a basic source of this differential. He said:
For "Maverick" sales to be made in volume in the U.S. market the car must be priced competitively with other cars in the Ford range and competitive cars of other makes. Since the general level of prices is still lower in the U.S. than in Canada this results in a differential pricing situation between the two countries.
It is not the government's policy to intervene in this pricing process unless there is evidence of serious distortion. The pricing of particular models is a matter for company decisions, decisions which are governed by the normal constraints of competition and

INDIAN AFFAIRS-BAND COUNCIL BORROWING REGULATIONS-PROVISION OF FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 21 I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) a question about the newly enacted regulations under the Indian Act entitled "Indian Band Council Borrowing Regulations" which appeared in the Canada Gazette, Part II, indicating that this was an entirely new set of regulations. Mr. Speaker suggested that it was a question that might be put on the order paper, but I felt that there are, or can be, important questions of public policy involved in these regulations; therefore, I thought it would be a suitable subject to raise at this time.
I notice that these regulations are made under section 72(l)(m) of the act. On checking the act I find that subsection (l)(m) was added to the act in 1956. I might draw to the attention of the House what seems to me to be a rather interesting parallel. The regulations read:
1.	These Regulations may be cited as the Indian Band Council Borrowing Regulations.
2.	The council of a band may borrow money for band projects or housing purposes and may make loans out of moneys so borrowed to members of the band for housing purposes, on such terms and conditions as may be determined by the council.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
On checking the legislative authority for these regulations I found that section 72 of
December 1, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations. Under subparagraph (m) the Governor in Council may make regulations for empowering and authorizing the council of a band to borrow money for band projects and housing and providing for the making of loans to members of the bands for housing purposes. It is obvious that the regulations are simply a re-enactment of the terms of the legislation which give this power to the Governor in Council.
The question which I feel should be answered is, naturally: What does the minister intend to accomplish through the passing of this set of regulations late in 1969, when authority was given to the Governor in Council in an amending act as long ago as 1956? It is true the authority has not been exercised either by Liberal or by Conservative governments in the intervening years.
One would have expected the regulations to expand somewhat on the provisions of the act. There are one or two questions which occur to me immediately. First, as I have mentioned, there is the question: What is the purpose of these regulations? We are all familiar with Indian needs and the limitation on their borrowing power because they are unable to make mortgaging arrangements in the ordinary way either as individuals or as a band. Are we to understand that the government is preparing, as suggested in my question, to set up a fund from which Indian bands might borrow at reasonable rates of interest under the terms of the regulations; or does the government have in mind making available some form of insurance guarantee such as is provided under various lending regulations so that, in effect, Indians can go into the public market when they want to borrow, with some kind of government guarantee behind them? I think this is a matter of general concern to members of the House and to all who are concerned with the possibility of the Indian people being able to proceed more directly to the management of their own affairs and the development of housing on the reserves in a self-sufficient way.
I again express the hope that the parliamentary secretary will be able to explain why the government should at this particular time have decided to act upon powers which were granted to it by Parliament as long ago as 1956.

Mr. Speaker, I can probably supply the information which the hon. member has requested. He should not be too concerned or even too critical of the fact that some time elapsed since the enabling legislation was passed and the regulations were promulgated. He will realise that in all areas of this government's legislative program, especially in the field of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, many new initiatives have been undertaken and many new programs are being proposed for discussion. This is the sort of thing that the government and the minister are doing to assist the native peoples of Canada.
